name: 80,000 Hours (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Moves people: each cause its plan changes go into, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: 80,000 Hours gives career research and advice (website, podcast, video, one-on-one advising, headhunting and a job board) to people who want to work on the most pressing problems, since 2025 mainly risks from advanced AI; it spent about $11.0M in 2025, nine months of it in its own audited accounts after leaving Effective Ventures. This model credits it with the careers it changed over 2012–2022 (its estimate of about 2,000 plan changes, against $18.8M spent), each valued by the site's shared career-change step: pay given up ($15,000 a year for five years) × the share it caused (40%, from its own criterion) × the value of a dollar of work in the causes its work now moves people into, read live (AI safety 90%, biosecurity and nuclear 6%, global health 2%, animal welfare 0.5%, our judgment), counted at the missing-data discount, net of a backfire share for roles that speed up AI, and at 36% for the next dollar against the 2012–2022 average. At the defaults it averts about 1.2 years of healthy life per $1,000 (0.06–24); most of that comes from the few careers outside AI, because the site's AI models come out low. The biggest uncertainties are the missing-data discount, the split by cause, the site's AI-risk and win-years sliders, what a plan change gives up and how much 80,000 Hours caused it, and the next dollar (it now spends five times its 2012–2022 yearly average).

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

source.title: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI-U annual averages (with facts/cpi.json from 2019)
source.note: Range ±2.5%: the spending's own exchange-rate uncertainty moves the weights little. Weights: 80,000 Hours' yearly spending 2012–2022 (financial accounts page). Sum of spending × factor = 22.476 ($M); ÷ 18.77 = 1.1974.

rows.explainer: Each year's spending inflated to 2025 prices by US consumer prices (Convention 8), weighted by that year's share of the period's spending: Σ spending_y × CPI_2025 / CPI_y ÷ Σ spending_y = $22.48M ÷ $18.77M. From 2019 the factors are the site's own (facts/cpi.json: 2019 1.259, 2020 1.244, 2021 1.188, 2022 1.100); before 2019 the BLS CPI-U annual averages chained to 2019 (2012 1.402 to 2018 1.282).

rows.label: Share of 2022's spending whose plan changes come after the end-2022 count
rows.explainer: Plan changes follow the advice that causes them: a job search takes months, a course application up to a year, and 80,000 Hours hears of many only later. With a lag of about six months on average, the changes bought by the second half of 2022's spending fall after the end-2022 count: half of 2022's spending is taken out of the period's cost. Our judgment, 0 (no lag) to 100% (a lag of a year or more).

rows.label: Value of a dollar of work in the causes 80,000 Hours' plan changes go into (live), units of value
rows.explainer: Where the people the next dollar moves go to work, by cause (our judgment of its work since its 2025 move to focus on AI, facts/meta.json eighty_k_career_share_*: AI safety 90%, biosecurity and nuclear 6%, global health 2%, animal welfare 0.5%; the rest, building effective altruism and research on priorities, takes the share-weighted average of these). The careers per dollar come from 2012–2022, when its advice was broader; the next dollar buys today's careers, so today's mix values them, each cause at the figure the rankings show for the charities of it the site models, under your values: AI safety the AI charities on the rankings, equal weights (#cause:ai); biosecurity and nuclear the biosecurity and the nuclear charities on the rankings, equal weights within each area and the two areas half each; global health GiveWell's Top Charities (value_global_health); animal welfare The Humane League (ACE's figure). By the site's rule for a split (normalization.md 2.8), here for careers rather than money.

rows.explainer: Valued by where this organisation's people go: its split by cause, each cause at its live result on this site (value_destinations). It moves no money (money_moved is 0); the new employers' value per dollar below reads this row.

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: an ordinary charity of its cause, as 1× GiveDirectly is in global health), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the shared rule for an organisation that moves money within a cause other than global health (catastrophic-risk). Shifted money was going to be given anyway, to an ordinary charity of the same cause; it is credited only for the gain. An ordinary charity stands to its cause's charities on the rankings as GiveDirectly (GiveWell's model, times a shared multiple, 1×, from 0 to 3×) stands to global health's: GiveDirectly's live result over the global-health charities' (#cause:global-health), times the catastrophic-risk charities' (#cause:catastrophic-risk), all live under your values.

Career plan changes 80,000 Hours caused, 2012 to 2022 (its estimate of the true number)

source.title: 80,000 Hours, Donate to 80,000 Hours
source.quote: We estimate that the true number of plan changes for this period was closer to 2,000, because we only expect to find out about a fraction of all plan changes.

rows.explainer: People who changed their career plans because of 80,000 Hours (a new job or a graduate course they say it had at least a 30% chance of causing, by its criteria, two-year review 2021–2022), counted over its first eleven years. It tracked 604 and estimates the true number at about 2,000, because it hears of only some of them: the range runs from the 604 it found (low) to half as many again as its estimate (high). Its own count: the advising calls, podcast and website reach many it never hears from.

rows.label: Career plan changes per year, 2012–2022 average
rows.explainer: A year's flow at the period's average, against a year's average cost above (templates.md Convention 3).

rows.label: Pay a career changer gives up per year (US$)
rows.explainer: The site's shared default ($15,000 a year, $5,000–30,000): 80,000 Hours publishes no salary survey of the people it moves. Its plan changes are often graduates and professionals moving into research and policy roles at charities and institutes that pay less than tech, finance or consulting; some move into well-paid jobs at AI companies and give up little, which the low end covers.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays in high-impact work
rows.explainer: The site's shared default (5 years, 2–10): 80,000 Hours publishes no follow-up of how long its plan changes stay in the work. Its plan changes are mostly early-career people choosing a path, which would argue for longer; some move on, which the low end covers.

rows.label: Years a career changer stays, discounted
rows.explainer: Discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Value of a dollar of the new employers' work (units of value)
rows.explainer: The jobs are spread over many employers in several causes, so the value of a dollar of their work is the causes' mix (moved_dollar_value, from value_destinations), each cause at its live figure.

rows.label: Share of the career changes the charity caused

source.title: 80,000 Hours, two-year review 2021–2022 (EA Forum post and full report)
source.quote: Within this we identified 266 who reported >30% chance of 80,000 Hours causing them to taking a new jobs or graduate course, which is the CBPC definition.

rows.explainer: 80,000 Hours' own: it counts a plan change only when the person reports at least a 30% chance it caused the change, so 30% is the floor of each counted case and the reported shares average above it (about half, our reading of the spread above the floor). People credit an adviser more than an outside view would, and many would have found similar work through the wider effective altruism community: × 0.8 for that, our judgment. 40%, from 20% (reports overstated by a third, below the floor) to 70% (reports taken at face value, many well above it). In place of the site's shared default, which is for charities without their own criterion.

rows.label: Value of one career change (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one career-change step (docs/normalization.md 2.8).

rows.label: Years from a plan change until the high-impact work starts
rows.explainer: Some plan changes are a graduate course, and the work it leads to starts years later; job changes start within months. 0.75 years on average, our judgment (about a quarter of changes being courses of two to four years), from 0 to 2; discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin (the site's missing-data step, docs/normalization.md 2.12): the count is 80,000 Hours' own estimate from self-reports (it tracked a third of it), with no controlled evaluation of its advice or content against people who didn't get it, and what a change is worth rests on the shared career defaults.

rows.label: Side benefits of the career changes and content, as a share of their value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the plan changes counted: people who take a pledge or start giving after its content without changing careers, and work others do better for its research without changing jobs. Earning-to-give plan changes are valued in the main chain like the others (their forgone pay standing in for their donations), not here. People who change careers without telling it are already in the 2,000. 10% (0–30%) of the modelled value, our judgment, anchored on Giving What We Can's 5% for its donors' wider influence (giving-what-we-can-charityevals) and set higher for its reach (578,733 engagement hours in 2024).

rows.label: Backfire of the career changes (work that speeds up dangerous AI), as a share of their value
rows.explainer: Its job board and advice send people to safety and policy roles at AI companies that also build more capable systems, which can speed that work up. A backfire of the work itself, so in the main chain (normalization.md 2.16). −10% (−40% to 0) of the modelled value, our judgment: the catastrophic-risk models' backfire step already nets a typical project's harm out of the AI figures, so this covers only roles more capabilities-adjacent than typical work (catastrophic-risk family, speedup_harm_share). Talent drawn from other good work is already netted by counting only forgone pay.

rows.label: Value of the career changes (units of value)
rows.explainer: The year's plan changes, each at the shared career-change value after the wait until the work starts, counted less for missing data, net of backfire and with their side benefits.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0, so this row multiplies nothing; the career branch has its own missing-data step (careers_missing_data_adj).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Total value (units of value)
rows.explainer: The adjustments apply to the policy and research branch; money moved counts its counterfactual through the shared new-money share (its dollars are measured, so no missing-data step), career changes through their own share and missing-data step.

rows.label: Value per dollar
rows.explainer: For WELLBYs, rename the uov_* rows to wellbys_* and report in wellby. For animals, rename them to sads_* and add the species section of the corporate-campaign template (output ced_per_donor_dollar). For climate, start from the climate skeleton.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost

source.title: 80,000 Hours, Financial accounts (spending by year, consolidated across the entities that ran it)
source.note: $18.77M / 91.5 staff-years = $205k per staff-year; 2025 budget staff costs $4.71M of $10.43M = 45%.

rows.explainer: Over 2012–2022 it spent $18.77M on 91.5 full-time staff-years (the same table's FTE column), about $205,000 per staff-year; at about $100,000 of pay and on-costs per staff-year for a UK and US research team, staff are about half of costs. Its 2025 budget puts staff at 45% ($4.71M of $10.43M), with marketing now a larger share than in the period. 50%, from 40% to 65%, our judgment (the $100,000 is our assumption, not a published figure). It matters only with credit by share of resources on.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: The shared pay gap for research and policy staff (@staff_pay.gap_research_policy): its staff are researchers, writers, advisers and podcast and video producers, many of whom could earn more in technology, media or consulting.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff (in-kind donation)
How much the next dollar does compared with the average dollar so far
rows.explainer: 80,000 Hours' own figure (facts/next_dollar.json): 36% (15–75%). The result is its 2012–2022 average; it now spends five times that period's yearly average and has a year of grants confirmed, so the next dollar does much less than the average one.
